notes: Ruling slot 3: Ramgoolam's Labour Party. Real coalition partner since late 1969 is the PMSD (Gaëtan Duval), placed in slot 1 (conservative); CAM, the third coalition party, in slot 2. Template coalition slot 18 holds the MMM per MD, although it is in opposition. IFB (opposition since the 1969 reshuffle) in slot 14. Slot 22 Special Mobile Force; slot 23 the Crown (Elizabeth II as Queen of Mauritius).

0.name: Le Parti de l'Ordre
0.text:
Le Parti de l'Ordre, 'the Party of Order', is the informal alliance of senior police officers, sugar-estate managers and conservative ministers who were shaken by the communal riots of January 1968 and the rise of militant students in 1969. They meet in the clubs of Curepipe and the offices of Port Louis.

They favour emergency powers, restrictions on strikes and radical meetings, and a government of national unity that keeps the opposition out for years. Firmly pro-Western, they welcome the British and American interest in the Chagos and Indian Ocean, and their leverage lies in the police, the estates and the coalition cabinet.

1.name: Parti Mauricien Social Démocrate
1.text:
The Mauritian Social Democratic Party, led by the flamboyant lawyer Gaëtan Duval, opposed independence and won some 44 percent of the vote in 1967 as the party of the Franco-Mauritians, Creoles and many Muslims and Sino-Mauritians. In late 1969 it joined Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam in a coalition government, with Duval as Minister of Foreign Affairs.

The PMSD stands for free enterprise, the sugar economy, close ties with France, Britain and the West, and the protection of minorities against Hindu majority rule. Its strength lies in the towns of the plateau, the Creole working class and the business community.

2.name: Comité d'Action Musulman
2.text:
The Muslim Committee of Action, led by Abdool Razack Mohamed, represents Indo-Mauritian Muslims and has been the faithful ally of the Labour Party since the 1950s. It fought the 1967 election inside the Independence Party alliance and holds seats and ministerial office in Ramgoolam's government.

The CAM stands for guaranteed representation of the Muslim community, protection of Muslim schools and personal law, and pragmatic, moderate politics that keep the community inside the governing coalition. Pro-Western and pro-Commonwealth, it trades its loyalty for patronage, and its leverage lies in the Muslim vote of Port Louis and several rural constituencies.

3.name: Parti Travailliste
3.text:
The Labour Party, founded in 1936 by Dr Maurice Curé to defend sugar workers and the poor, has been led by Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam since the 1950s. It led the island to independence on 12 March 1968, and Ramgoolam governs as Prime Minister in a coalition with the PMSD and the Muslim Committee of Action.

Labour stands for a welfare state, wider education, rural development and moderate Fabian socialism within the Commonwealth and a pro-Western foreign policy. Its base is the Hindu rural majority, the sugar-estate workers and the trade unions, and its leverage lies in Ramgoolam's prestige as father of the nation.

4.name: Cercle Lénine
4.text:
The Cercle Lénine is a small group of orthodox Marxist-Leninists among trade unionists, teachers and returned students from Europe and the Soviet Union, who meet in Port Louis and the industrial suburbs. It looks to Moscow and the French Communist Party for its doctrine.

The circle calls for nationalisation of the sugar estates and the banks, a planned economy, a workers' front against the 'communal' parties and friendship with the Soviet Union. Distrusted by the government and overshadowed by the new militant movement, its leverage lies in a few docks and transport unions and its contacts abroad.

5.name: Zenes Militan
5.text:
Zenes Militan, 'the Militant Youth', are the radical students, young teachers and unemployed graduates who burst into politics in 1969, staging protests during Princess Alexandra's visit and filling the meetings of the new militant movement. Many have returned from Paris after May 1968.

They want to sweep away communal politics, nationalise the sugar industry, promote Kreol as the national language and break with Britain and the United States over Diego Garcia. More impatient than the MMM leadership, they favour strikes and street action, and their leverage lies in the colleges and the unemployed youth of the towns.

6.name: Sanatan Shakti
6.text:
Sanatan Shakti, 'Sanatan Strength', is a hardline current of orthodox Hindu priests, temple committee elders and village notables who fear that Westernisation, Christian missions and secular radicals threaten the faith of the Indo-Mauritian majority. They look to India rather than Britain for cultural guidance.

They want Hindu values to shape national life, support for temples and Hindi schooling, stricter morality and distance from Western influence, and they welcome India's friendship with the Soviet Union over alignment with Washington. Their leverage lies in the baitkas, temples and caste associations of the rural north and centre.

7.name: Bann Taper
7.text:
Bann Taper, 'the Strongmen', are the party bosses, ward organisers and hired toughs who ran the street side of Mauritian politics through the 1960s and fought in the communal clashes of 1965 and 1968. They now serve whichever patron in government pays and protects them.

They want permanent one-party government by the coalition, no elections that might bring the militants to power, and a free hand against opponents. Indifferent to ideology yet hostile to Western liberal scruples, their leverage lies in intimidation at the polling stations and in the protection of politicians who need their services.

8.name: Idara-e-Imamia
8.text:
Idara-e-Imamia is the welfare and study body of the small Twelver Shia community of Mauritius, mostly families of Gujarati and Bombay merchant origin in Port Louis and Rose Hill. It organises Muharram majalis, religious classes and charity, and keeps ties with Khoja jamaats in East Africa.

Its leaders favour an educated, reform-minded faith, good relations with the much larger Sunni community and loyal cooperation with the government. Politically cautious, they seek recognition of Shia festivals and burial grounds, and their leverage lies in their commercial standing and their families' connections with the coalition parties.

9.name: Tanzeem-e-Hussaini
9.text:
Tanzeem-e-Hussaini is a small group of young Shia men in Port Louis who studied in Najaf, Qom or Karachi and came back convinced that the faith must be led by militant clergy rather than merchant elders. They gather around cassette sermons from Iraq and Iran.

They hold that learned jurists must guide Muslim life, condemn the Shah as a servant of the West and want stricter religious discipline and separation from secular society. With no foothold in the coalition and little standing in their own community, their leverage is limited to a few households and to contacts with clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Jummah Mosque
10.text:
The Jummah Mosque of Port Louis, built in the nineteenth century by Indian Muslim merchants, is the most important mosque on the island and the seat of the Sunni religious establishment. Its trustees, imams and allied ulama speak for the traditional piety of the Indo-Mauritian Muslim community.

The establishment is loyal and conservative: it supports the government and the Muslim Committee of Action, defends Muslim personal law, madrasas and endowments and keeps clear of radical politics. Its leverage lies in its trust funds, its pulpit and its authority over the religious life of the island's Muslims.

11.name: Halqat al-Tahrir
11.text:
Halqat al-Tahrir is a tiny clandestine circle of young Muslims in Port Louis and Plaine Verte who discovered Hizb ut-Tahrir literature through contacts in London and the Middle East. It meets in private homes and has no public organisation.

Its members reject elections, communal parties and both superpowers, and preach a single caliphate uniting the Muslim world. In multi-religious Mauritius they find few listeners and avoid open confrontation, limiting themselves to study circles and recruitment among students, but they regard the island's Muslims as part of an umma that will one day rise again.

12.name: Halqa-e-Islami
12.text:
Halqa-e-Islami is a circle of educated young Muslims in Port Louis and Rose Hill, many of them teachers and civil servants, who read Maududi and Hasan al-Banna and want an organised, socially engaged Islam beyond the conservative mosque committees and the patronage of the Muslim Committee of Action.

It promotes Islamic education, welfare work, moral reform and Arabic and Urdu teaching, accepts parliamentary politics and supports the Palestinian cause. Neutral between the blocs, it hopes to give Muslims a principled rather than merely communal voice, and its leverage lies in a growing following among young professionals and students.

13.name: Les Mandarins
13.text:
Les Mandarins are the senior civil servants, permanent secretaries and planners who run the young state, many trained in Britain and still working with British advisers. Under the coalition of national unity they have become the quiet power behind ministers who rarely master their files.

They favour order, planning, export-processing industry and family planning to contain population growth, and see party competition as a distraction from development. Non-aligned in outlook and pragmatic toward all donors, their leverage lies in controlling budgets, appointments and the drafting of every law.

14.name: Independent Forward Bloc
14.text:
The Independent Forward Bloc was founded in 1958 by Sookdeo Bissoondoyal, a teacher and leader of the Hindu revivalist and rural movement. It fought the 1967 election inside the Independence Party alliance with Labour but left government as the coalition was reshaped around the PMSD in 1969 and now sits in opposition.

The IFB speaks for small Hindu planters, labourers and villagers, demanding land for smallholders, fair cane prices, Hindi and Bhojpuri culture and an end to the privileges of the sugar oligarchy. Its leverage lies in the villages of the north and in its claim to represent the rural poor that Labour neglects.

15.name: Chambre d'Agriculture de l'île Maurice
15.text:
The Mauritius Chamber of Agriculture, founded in 1853, is the voice of the Franco-Mauritian sugar barons who own the great estates and mills that produce nearly all the island's exports. Its members are among the richest families in the Indian Ocean.

The Chamber defends the sugar quota under the Commonwealth Sugar Agreement, opposes land reform and nationalisation, and quietly finances parties that protect property, today chiefly the PMSD. Its leverage is immense: the estates employ a large share of the workforce, earn the foreign exchange and control the credit on which the whole economy depends.

16.name: Chinese Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Chinese Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1908, represents the Sino-Mauritian shopkeepers, importers and wholesalers whose village stores reach every corner of the island. The community is small but economically indispensable and aligned with the Republic of China on Taiwan.

The Chamber wants free trade, low taxes, easy credit and security for property, and fears both nationalisation and the radicalism of the new militant movement. It avoids open partisanship, though many members lean to the PMSD, and its leverage lies in the retail and credit network on which rural Mauritians depend for daily goods.

17.name: Royal Society of Arts and Sciences of Mauritius
17.english: Royal Society of Arts and Sciences of Mauritius
17.text:
The Royal Society of Arts and Sciences of Mauritius, heir to the natural history society founded in 1829, is the island's oldest learned body and home to its naturalists, foresters and historians. Its members document the remnants of native forest and the rare endemic birds, from the kestrel to the pink pigeon.

The Society calls for nature reserves, protection of the last upland forests and offshore islets, control of invasive species and scientific cooperation with international conservation bodies. Its leverage lies in scientific authority and foreign interest, though it competes with the sugar estates and planters for every acre of land.

18.name: Mouvement Militant Mauricien
18.text:
The Mauritian Militant Movement was founded in 1969 by young radicals around Paul Bérenger, Dev Virahsawmy and Jooneed Jeeroburkhan, who emerged from student activism. On 1 January 1970 it is a fast-growing opposition movement rallying those who reject both the coalition and communal politics.

The MMM stands for a non-communal socialism, nationalisation of the sugar industry and key sectors, workers' rights, Kreol as a national language and a non-aligned foreign policy, including the return of the Chagos Archipelago. Its leverage lies among the youth, the dockers and the urban workers who see the coalition as a club of old elites.

19.name: Ligne Rouge
19.text:
Ligne Rouge, 'the Red Line', is a small Maoist tendency of students, teachers and young intellectuals in Port Louis and Rose Hill, many returned from France, who consider the Moscow-oriented left revisionist and the new militant movement too ready to compromise with parliament.

They call for a revolution of sugar workers and small planters against the estate owners, the Chinese road of self-reliance, total rupture with Britain and the United States and solidarity with the liberation struggles of the Third World. Their leverage lies in student committees and a few militant cells among estate labourers.

20.name: Les Mauriciens d'Abord
20.text:
Les Mauriciens d'Abord, 'Mauritians First', is a populist current among Creole and Franco-Mauritian voters who felt betrayed when the PMSD entered government with Labour after campaigning against independence and Hindu dominance. It draws on the fear and anger that drove thousands to emigrate after 1967.

It rails against what it calls Hindu hegemony, communal patronage and the coalition's 'sell-out', demands law and order, jobs for local people and an end to political favouritism, and distrusts the radical left. Its leverage lies in the disillusioned towns of the plateau and among those still weighing departure for Australia.

21.name: Ordre et Patrie
21.text:
Ordre et Patrie, 'Order and Fatherland', is a fringe of ultra-conservative toughs, ex-servicemen and admirers of authoritarian European regimes who emerged from the vigilante groups of the 1968 riots. They train in private, wear the language of discipline and see democracy as the road to chaos.

They want strong rule by a single leader, a ban on the militant left and the communal parties alike, and a disciplined nation under martial values. Tiny but violent, they despise both Moscow and liberal democracy, and their leverage lies in intimidation and in sympathies among some police and estate security men.

22.name: Special Mobile Force
22.text:
The Special Mobile Force, formed in 1960 as the paramilitary arm of the Mauritius Police Force, is the closest thing the island has to an army. It is still partly officered by Britons and was reinforced by British troops during the communal riots of January 1968.

Its officers see themselves as guardians of order against communal violence, strikes and the radical left, and their loyalty runs to the government of the day and to the British connection. Their leverage lies in the only trained, armed and mobile force on the island, decisive in any crisis in Port Louis.

23.name: The Crown
23.text:
Since independence in 1968 Mauritius has been a Commonwealth realm with Queen Elizabeth II as Queen of Mauritius, represented by the Governor-General, Sir Leonard Williams. The Crown remains a symbol of continuity for Franco-Mauritians, Creoles and many others who feared independence.

Its supporters defend the monarchy, the link with Britain and the Commonwealth, an impartial head of state and the rule of law, and oppose talk of a republic from the militant left. Their leverage lies in the Governor-General's constitutional reserve powers and in the loyalty of the minorities who see the Crown as a guarantee against majority domination.
